findings.headline: Pass reconcile's key as a string; Solid 2 takes no options object.
findings.why: reconcile gets { key: "id", merge: true }. Solid 1.x's reconcile(value, { key, merge }) took an options object; Solid 2.0.3's reconcile(value, key) takes the key (a property name or a function of the item) as its second argument and returns a draft function, so setStore(reconcile(value, key)) stays valid.
findings.guidance: Replace the options object with its key: reconcile(value, { key: "id" }) becomes reconcile(value, "id"), and { key: null } becomes null. Solid 2 has no merge option; if the code relied on merge: true, stop and ask how the store's consumers use object identity before choosing a replacement.

findings.headline: Rewrite this object-merge store setter call as draft assignments.
findings.why: The argument is a call expression. Solid 2.0.3's plain store setter accepts only a draft callback, setStore(state => { ... }); Solid 1.x also accepted a path followed by a value, an object to merge, and a function whose returned object was merged into the store, while a value returned from the 2.0 draft callback is adopted as the whole new state instead.
findings.guidance: Read the argument and the store shape. Replace the call with setStore(state => { ... }) that assigns each top-level key of the argument onto the draft; nested objects that 1.x merged shallowly must be assigned per key too if other keys at that level must survive.
